key_findings.finding: Exogenous insulin is unlikely because exogenous insulin should suppress endogenous C-peptide and proinsulin; the simultaneous presence of both favors endogenous secretion. Autoimmune hypoglycemia remains possible only if insulin autoantibodies are positive, but typical insulin autoimmune syndrome often shows marked insulin elevation, assay/insulin-antibody abnormalities, and frequently postprandial or fluctuating hypoglycemia.

source_tools.relevance: The autoimmune-hypoglycemia literature identifies insulin autoantibodies as the defining mediator and discusses characteristic insulin/C-peptide discordance and assay interference.

source_tools.relevance: The NIPHS literature describes endogenous hyperinsulinemia with elevated insulin/C-peptide and low beta-hydroxybutyrate, but the retrieved cases emphasize the syndrome as a distinct diagnosis requiring clinical-context evaluation, including post-bariatric/postprandial settings.
